query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, phase stability is governed by the degree of local chemical ordering induced by aluminum’s large atomic size mismatch, which promotes nanoscale ordered domains (e.g., B2 or L12 precipitates) within a primarily FCC matrix. These ordered regions act as structural mediators that restrict dislocation motion and modify defect interactions, thereby jointly enhancing high‐temperature strength, environmental and radiation resistance, and cryogenic toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase equiatomic FCC Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloy with minimal local chemical ordering.
generation.intervention: Systematic variation of aluminum content and controlled thermal treatments to trigger local chemical ordering and the formation of nanoscale ordered precipitates.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted under controlled inert atmospheres with annealing treatments spanning high temperatures (for defect activation and ordering kinetics) as well as cryogenic mechanical tests, ensuring comparable strain rates and environmental conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale ordered domains (e.g., B2 or L12 precipitates) that develop via aluminum-induced local chemical ordering and lattice distortion.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum, due to its larger atomic size relative to the transition metals, increases local lattice distortions. Under appropriate thermal conditions, this drives short-range chemical ordering that results in the precipitation of ordered nanodomains. These domains serve as barriers to dislocation motion and help arrest radiation-induced defect propagation, thereby enhancing the strength and toughness balance over a wide temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with an optimized, moderate aluminum addition will display a dual-phase microstructure identifiable by X-ray diffraction and TEM (e.g., split or superlattice peaks) accompanied by enhanced high-temperature yield strength, improved radiation resistance, and elevated fracture toughness at cryogenic temperatures relative to the single-phase baseline alloy.
generation.baseline: The single-phase equiatomic FCC alloy with lower aluminum-induced chemical ordering exhibits lower strength at high temperatures and reduced damage tolerance under cryogenic conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies specifically within the compositional space near equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys where aluminum can be varied without inducing a complete structural transition (e.g., to a fully brittle BCC phase). It may not hold for compositions with excessive aluminum content or markedly different alloying ratios.
generation.uncertainty: The precise aluminum concentration threshold that maximizes beneficial local ordering without promoting unwanted brittle phase formation remains to be determined, as does the quantitative impact of the ordered nanodomains on radiation tolerance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA samples: one set with a baseline (minimal Al-induced ordering) composition and the other with an optimized, moderately increased aluminum content subjected to identical thermal annealing. Characterize the microstructures using X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy to detect the presence of ordered nanodomains. Perform mechanical tests (tensile tests at high temperatures and fracture toughness tests at cryogenic temperatures) and radiation exposure experiments to compare performance.
measurements: XRD patterns to identify superlattice reflections or peak splitting indicative of ordering
TEM imaging to resolve nanoscale ordered domains
Mechanical properties (yield strength, tensile strength, fracture toughness) at high and low temperatures
Radiation-induced defect density measurements post irradiation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the optimized-aluminum HEA does not show any detectable nanoscale ordered domains relative to the baseline (via XRD/TEM) or if no corresponding improvement in high-temperature strength, radiation resistance, and cryogenic toughness is observed between the two sets, then the hypothesis that aluminum-induced local ordering stabilizes the phase and improves these properties is falsified.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs), composed of five or more principal elements in near-equiatomic ratios, have attracted widespread attention due to their unique combination of high strength and toughness [,,]. Unlike conventional alloys, which are typically based on one or two major elements, HEAs are stabilized by high mixing entropy, lowering the Gibbs free energy and favoring the formation of simple solid solution phases. In addition to their excellent mechanical properties, HEAs also demonstrate superior thermal stability and corrosion resistance, making them highly suitable for use in harsh environments such as aerospace, nuclear power systems, and marine engineering [,]. Among the various HEA systems, FeCoNiCrMn has emerged as one of the most extensively studied, featuring a stable FCC structure []. Furthermore, refractory HEAs such as TiNbZrMoV and MoNbTaVW primarily form a single BCC solid solution and exhibit excellent high-temperature strength and phase stability [,].

Compared to high-entropy alloys, medium-entropy alloys exhibit lower mixing entropy, typically ranging from R to 1.5R (where R is the gas constant). MEAs generally comprise three to four principal elements in near-equiatomic proportions, representing an intermediate class of multi-component alloys that bridge the gap between conventional alloys and HEAs [,]. Unlike HEAs, MEAs possess relatively lower compositional complexity, which allows for better control over microstructure and phase stability while still retaining desirable mechanical and thermal properties. Among these, CoCrNi-based MEAs have attracted considerable attention in recent years, driven by their promising performance and the rapid increase in related research efforts [,,]. They exhibit not only excellent mechanical strength and ductility at elevated temperatures but also outstanding fracture toughness at cryogenic temperatures [].

Equiatomic multi-component metallic materials, referred to variously as high-entropy alloys (HEAs), multi-component alloys or compositionally complex alloys, have generated considerable excitement in the materials science community of late as a new class of materials that derive their properties not from a single dominant constituent, such as iron in steels, but rather from multiple principal elements with the potential for unique combinations of mechanical properties compared with conventional alloys. They have attracted increasing attention, especially as structural materials, due to their remarkable mechanical strength and resistance to oxidation and fatigue at ambient and elevated temperatures. There has been a notable increase of interest in the high-entropy alloys (HEAs) in the last years due to their outstanding properties, e.g., excellent strength and fracture toughness, high hardness, good wear and corrosion resistance, and good thermal conductivity. The HEAs contain several elements in equimolar or near equimolar ratios that often possess different ground state crystal structures. However, the majority of these reported alloys exhibit two simple structures, i.e., face-centered cubic (fcc) or body-centered cubic (bcc), whereas only few single-phase HEAs with hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structure have been produced. Among those, the hcp HEAs containing rare earth elements did not show compositional segregation, e.g., DyGdHoTbY, but they typically lacked pronounced solid-solution hardening due to the similar size and electronic structure of the constituents. Attempts to synthesize single-phase hcp HEAs without rare earth elements have been rare until now owing to compositional segregation.

Recent developments of high-entropy alloys with high strength and high ductility draw attention to the metastability-engineering strategy. Using first-principle theory, here we demonstrate that reducing the Ta level in the refractory TiZrHfTax system destabilizes the body-centered cubic (bcc) phase and leads to the appearance of the hexagonal close-packed (hcp) phase embedded in the bcc matrix. The alloying-induced features of the elastic parameters for the cubic and hexagonal structures are mapped out in details, and strong sensitivity to the crystal lattice and chemistry is revealed. Results show softening of the bcc matrix with decreasing Ta concentration which ensures ductile behavior. However, the elastically nearly isotropic hcp precipitates possess enhanced resistance against shear which promotes strengthening of the TiZrHfTax dual-phase system. The present atomic-level insight provides strong evidence to the experimental observation, and emphasizes the significance of quantum-design for advanced multi-phase high-entropy alloys with excellent strength-ductility combinations.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs), which were originally developed as concentrated solid solutions of multiple principal elements in equal, or near equal, atomic ratios, have drawn progressively increasing attention over the past decade. Unlike single principal-element alloys, their complex alloy compositions and elemental distribution, together with crystal lattice distortion induced by atomic-size mismatch (depending upon relative atomic sizes), can have a significant effect on the activity of their crystal defects and hence mechanical properties. Although HEAs were initially designed to benefit from single-phase stabilization,, single-phase HEAs are actually not that common, and of those that do exist, only a few display excellent damage-tolerance in the form of combinations of high strength, ductility, and toughness. AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties

High-entropy alloys have good application prospects in nuclear power plants due to their excellent mechanical properties and radiation resistance. In this paper, the microstructure of the Co32Cr28Ni32.94Al4.06Ti3 high-entropy alloy was researched using metallurgical microscopy, X-ray diffraction, and scanning electron microscopy. The mechanical properties were tested using a Vickers microhardness tester and a tensile testing machine, respectively. The results showed that Co32Cr28Ni32.94Al4.06Ti3 had a single-phase, disordered, face-centered, cubic solid-solution structure and was strengthened by solid solution. The alloy lattice parameter and density were estimated as 0.304 nm and 7.89 g/cm3, respectively. The test results indicated that the alloy had satisfactory mechanical properties with yield stress and tensile strength of about 530 MPa and 985 MPa, respectively.

High-entropy alloys are composed of a minimum of five components, whose concentrations are approximately between 5 and 35 at.%. HEAs show some distinct features, for example, excellent mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, wear resistance, and high temperature oxidation properties. Since the high-entropy alloys may have various outstanding properties, they are of considerable importance in engineering applications [,,]. In the study of the HEAs containing aluminum by transmission electron microscope (TEM) observations, phase transformations—such as precipitation transformation [,,], spinodal decomposition [,,,,], and ordering reaction [,]—were found, and their product phases were L12 [,,], and B2 [,,,,,] superlattices.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs), a kind of novel alloy formed by mixing equal or relatively large proportions of several elements, have attracted much academic and industrial attention since they were first developed in 2004. HEAs exhibit many unique advantages such as high strength and high resistance to corrosion/wear, compared with conventional alloys. These excellent properties make HEAs widely expected as the structural material used in the high-temperature and corrosive environments, e.g., high-temperature and high-pressure water environment in power plants.
